nodes.question: What was the estimated contribution of CT and MR imaging to total carbon dioxide emissions in 2016?
nodes.answer: CT and MR imaging were estimated to contribute up to 0.77% of total carbon dioxide emissions in 2016.
nodes.paragraph: As healthcare professionals, wecan protect our patients by responding to the health effects of climate change and other environmental expo- sures and signal the importance of an urgent transition to environmentally sustainable imaging practice [ 3]. The delivery of healthcare generates substantial greenhousegas emissions, with diagnostic services accounting forapproximately 9% of healthcare emissions in one region inAustralia [ 4]. Globally, CT and MR imaging were esti- mated to contribute up to 0.77% of total carbon dioxideemissions for 2016 with an expected 30% growth between 2016 and 2030 [ 5,6]. nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How much of the total emissions do municipally owned facilities contribute?
nodes.answer: Municipally owned facilities contribute only 5% of a community's total emissions.
nodes.paragraph: In this research, we ask to what extent city CAPs can contribute to meaningful climate action at the local level. Through a review of CAPs published by U.S. cities between 2018 and early 2023, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of these documents to better understand the current state of climate action planning, to ask how U.S. cities are approaching climate action, and to make recommenda - tions to strengthen both research and practice. 1.1 Background on climate action planning As an initial step in the climate action planning process, cities measure and report their GHG emissions through a GHG inventory. Urban regions are key sources of emissions, accounting for over 70% of total GHG emissions (Ruth et al. 2017 ; United Nations 2019 ). Three sectors accounted for 77% of total GHG emissions in the United States: Transporta - tion (28%), Electric Power (25%), and Industry (23%) (U.S. EPA 2024). Conversely, munic - ipally owned facilities only account for 5% of a community S total emissions. (City of Raleigh 2016 ).

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the main challenge with sector-based emissions inventories according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main challenge is that sector-based emissions inventories lack a comprehensive view of a city's true metabolism.
nodes.paragraph: While tracking emissions by sector appears as a simple accounting exercise, the practice can be complicated by consumption-based accounting. Emissions are most often reported on a per sector basis, but such sector-based emissions inventories lack a comprehensive view of a city S true metabolism (C40 2018 ). C40 Cities recommends consumption-based inventories, which also include emissions from all goods and services produced and con- sumed within a city (C40 2018). Such accounting can greatly increase reported emissions. For instance, the City of Portland saw a 118% increase in emissions after conducting a consumption-based inventory (City of Portland and Multnomah County 2015 ). Consider - ing such drastic increases when cities utilize a consumption-based emissions inventory, the 1 5% of municipal facilities share of local emissions would shrink even further as a true contribution to its community S total emissions. Upon the completion of a GHG inventory, cities develop mitigation and adaptation strategies for meeting emissions reduction targets and responding to future climate impacts (Boswell et al. 2010 ; Alloisio and Borghesi 2020 ). In the U.S., cities have primarily focused their actions on mitigating climate change.
